answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Mae West and entirely consistent with her habit of flipping stern proverbs into come-ons — but no primary source pins this exact line. Wikiquote files it under “Unsourced” ↗, and popular claims that it comes from her 1959 memoir or a 1930s film remain undocumented.

source.excerpt: Too much of a good thing can be wonderful.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line among Mae West’s “Unsourced” quotations ↗ — no cited film, book, or recording.
The Quotations Page records the shorter variant “Too much of a good thing is wonderful” ↗, crediting Mae West but naming no work.
The gag reworks an old English proverb whose earliest print example is Shakespeare’s As You Like It (1600) ↗, where Rosalind asks “can one desire too much of a good thing?”
source.excerptNote: Also circulates in the shorter form “Too much of a good thing is wonderful.” Both are Mae West’s deliberate flip of the centuries-old warning that one can have too much of a good thing.
source.rightsNote: The exact first appearance of this wording has not been documented, so no copyright status can be asserted. If it is genuinely Mae West’s, every plausible source — her 1930s Paramount films, her 1959 memoir, or a later compiled collection — was first published after 1931 and would remain in copyright to the Mae West estate and/or original publisher, not public domain.

author.name: Mae West
author.heading: Who was Mae West?
author.metaLine: 1893–1980 · American actress, playwright and vaudeville-bred wit
author.bio: Mae West was an American actress, screenwriter and playwright who turned double-entendre into an art form on the vaudeville stage, in her own scandal-courting Broadway plays, and in 1930s Paramount films such as She Done Him Wrong and I’m No Angel. She wrote most of her own dialogue, and her comic method was to take a piece of received wisdom and flip it into something knowing and appetitive. So many quips are pinned on her that a West-sounding line and a documented one are not always the same thing.

cite.sourceCitation: Attributed to Mae West (1893–1980). Widely quoted from the mid-20th century onward and often linked — without confirmation — to her memoir Goodness Had Nothing to Do with It (Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Prentice-Hall, 1959); recorded as unsourced in Wikiquote. The line inverts the proverb best known from Shakespeare’s As You Like It (1600).

misattribution.heading: The catch: everyone names a source, no one can show it
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Mae West is plausible and unchallenged — the problem is the false precision bolted onto it. Quote sites confidently name a book or film that none of them can actually cite.

items.why: Aggregators variously assign the line to Goodness Had Nothing to Do with It (1959) or to a Paramount picture, but none pins a page or scene, and Wikiquote keeps it in the “Unsourced” column ↗.
It travels as both “can be wonderful” and the tighter “is wonderful” ↗ — a sign it was passed around by ear rather than copied from a fixed text.
The joke depends on a warning far older than West — that you can have too much of a good thing — whose earliest print form is Shakespeare’s As You Like It (1600) ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Best read as a genuine Mae West quip in spirit — hers by style and long association — but one whose exact wording sits undocumented in the record ↗, reworking a proverb centuries older than she was.

context.heading: Why it sounds like her
lead: Mae West built a career on inversion: taking the prim moral of a proverb and turning it into an invitation. “Too much of a good thing can be wonderful” is that engine in one line — it answers the old caution that you can overdo pleasure with a flat, delighted “yes, and?”

That is exactly why it resists verification. The line is so perfectly in character that quote collectors reached for a source after the fact, attaching her memoir or a film without ever showing the words on a page. The honest position: the sentiment is unmistakably Westian, but the citation is missing.
detailsBody: The phrase “too much of a good thing” was already proverbial by the late 15th century. Its most famous early appearance is in Shakespeare’s As You Like It (c. 1600), when Rosalind teases, “Why then, can one desire too much of a good thing?” For centuries it carried a note of warning. West’s contribution — whenever she first said it — was to strip the warning out entirely.
context.pull: She didn’t coin the proverb — she coined the comeback to it.
